title: The War Between Open Source, Open Weight, And Closed AI Models
gist: Timothy Prickett Morgan argues the closed vs open-weight vs fully-open-source model fight will resolve the way operating systems did — open wins once it reaches functional parity — and that Nvidia is the only vendor rich enough to give away code, weights and datasets (Nemotron 3) because its hardware margins pay for it. The article's punchline is a fork: if distillation lets all models average toward each other, only inference hardware can be charged for ('Advantage, Nvidia'); if closed models stay measurably better, API and on-prem licensing survives. Note an internal inconsistency in the text: the opening calls Llama 3 and 4 'fully open source' while a later paragraph states explicitly they were open weight, not open sourced.

insights.claim: In high-stakes verticals like medical imaging, end users never choose which AI model is used — medical software suppliers and healthcare companies make the open/closed/open-weight decision on their behalf, making ISVs and health IT vendors the real demand aggregators for foundation models.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Model distribution in regulated verticals is won by selling to application vendors, not end customers — watch ISV model-partnership announcements as the leading indicator of enterprise inference share.

insights.claim: The market splits into three legally and commercially distinct tiers — closed proprietary (OpenAI, Anthropic), open weight but not open source (Meta, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, DeepSeek, OpenAI, Google, Mistral, Hugging Face uploads), and fully open source including source, weights and training datasets (Nvidia's Nemotron 3) — and conflating open weight with open source is the central confusion in the debate.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Use the three-tier split when underwriting 'open source AI' claims — only the fully-open tier removes vendor dependency, and almost nothing in the market qualifies.

insights.so_what: The parity test, not ideology, is the timing signal: track when open-weight models close the eval gap, because that is historically when proprietary pricing power breaks.

insights.claim: The Y2K-era ERP migration is the template for enterprise AI adoption: companies with heavy technical debt discarded in-house code for SAP, Oracle and Microsoft packages and reshaped their businesses around vendor software, trading control for speed and betting the vendor could ship features and security faster than they could.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: If AI repeats the ERP path, value accrues to incumbent application suites that bolt on AI rather than to enterprises building bespoke stacks.
insights.quote: They traded control for speed, and are betting the application software providers can add features and provide security that they would have trouble doing in house.

insights.claim: Enterprises running third-party applications appear inclined to simply wait for their software partners to add AI features, while a separate cohort wants to own its AI stack and wrap it around existing ERP, SCM and CRM suites rather than gut them — the same split seen when web technologies were added to those suites.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Two distinct revenue pools: AI upsell inside incumbent suites, and a wrap-around tooling/inference layer sold to the own-your-stack cohort.

insights.claim: There is no free path in enterprise AI: either you invest in software developers and spend time, or you wait and pay the software houses, and the comparative math is rarely crisply clear.

insights.so_what: 'Free' open weights do not mean cheap deployment — the labor cost of self-hosting is what determines whether open models actually undercut API pricing.

insights.claim: Nvidia is probably the only company that can afford full openness — releasing source code, weights and the training datasets for its Nemotron 3 models — because its hardware pricing subsidizes the software giveaway.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Nvidia can commoditize the model layer at will, compressing pure-play model vendors' pricing while defending its own hardware margin.

insights.claim: Given what customers pay for Nvidia hardware, the accompanying software should effectively be free — a direct rerun of the IBM System/360 model six decades ago, where IBM sent in programmer teams and application code was open to users because the hardware carried the margin.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Frames free models as a hardware-attach tactic — expect more vendor-funded open releases wherever a hardware or cloud margin can absorb the cost.

insights.so_what: Direct competitive pressure on commercial agent-orchestration startups whose product is now available free from the chip supplier.

insights.claim: Meta Platforms has repeatedly flip-flopped on openness — closed initial AI models, open weight (not open source) with Llama 3 launched February 2023 and expanded April 2024, bigger but still only open-weight Llama 4, a closed Spark 1.1 launched April 2026, an open-weight 1.2 promised, and the 30-billion-parameter single-GPU Muse Glimmer released open weight from the start.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Meta's openness is tactical and reversible, so any competitive plan that assumes free frontier weights from Meta carries policy risk at every release.
insights.locator: The company kept its initial AI models closed and proprietary

insights.claim: Meta's earlier openness — Open Compute Project hardware, the React JavaScript generator and the PyTorch AI framework — was driven by enlightened self-interest, opening code specifically to get outside programmers building interfaces and AI the Meta way.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Read every open-source release as a standard-setting play: the giver is buying ecosystem lock-in, which tells you what it plans to monetize later.
insights.quote: These were opened for very self-serving reasons – to get programmers to do interfaces and AI the Meta Platforms way – and there is absolutely nothing wrong with enlightened self-interest.

insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Small-model economics are downstream of frontier capex — restricting distillation would break the cheap end of the market, not just the copycats.

insights.claim: Mark Zuckerberg is publicly lobbying for US policy to permit distillation and broad data use in training, arguing that models learning from other models is a core principle of the open source ecosystem and that restricting it would cost the US its lead.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A US regulatory fight over distillation and training-data rights is forming; its outcome determines whether frontier labs can defend model IP at all.
insights.quote: For the US to lead in open source, we will need to rethink our policies in several areas, including distillation and data use in training,

insights.claim: Zuckerberg frames the right to distill as a right to learn from anything observable, explicitly pushing back on the framing of distillation as harmful — while the author notes China has already been distilling from US models to train its own.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Any US ban on distillation would bind US labs while China distills regardless — a one-sided constraint worth pricing into frontier-lab moat assumptions.
insights.quote: Some have tried to frame distillation as harmful, but I think it is important to protect the principle that you can learn from anything you can observe.

insights.claim: If unrestricted distillation causes all models to average against each other, model quality converges and nothing above the inference hardware layer can command a price — the author's explicit conclusion is 'Advantage, Nvidia.'
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The bear case for model-layer margins is simultaneously the bull case for accelerators — model-quality convergence data is the variable to monitor.

insights.claim: The opposing scenario is that closed models sustain a measurable quality lead over open ones, in which case proprietary labs survive by selling API access broadly while also licensing models for on-premises deployment.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The binary is quality-gap persistence: closed labs need both API and on-prem licensing revenue to justify valuations if the gap narrows.
insights.quote: Then again, if the quality of the closed models can stay better than the open models, they can hang in there and sell API access to anyone and everyone and still license their models for on-premises use cases.
